**ticket-runner** `<version>` · run `<runId>` · `<branch>`

| Stage | Outcome | Context | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| verify | ❌ <k> unmet | <context> | <duration> |
| fix | ✅ committed | <context> · compacted | <duration> |
| verify | ✅ <k> met · <c> to CI · <u> unverifiable | <context> | <duration> |
| pr | ✅ revised | <context> | <duration> |
| conflict | ✅ rebased | <context> | <duration> |

| merge | ✅ #<pr> | – | – |

One section per Run that worked the Ticket, oldest first: the header naming
that Run's version, runId and branch, a blank line, and that Run's table. A
Ticket one Run took from the claim to the merge has one section.

One row per Stage or gate, appended as it finishes, in the order it happened.
Rows are not unique: a fix buys a second pass of verify, and each rebase
conflict adds a `conflict` row. The pipeline runs no Check on the branch, so no
row is a Check's: the pull request's CI, which the Target sets up, grades the
code on the `ci` row. A Stage that is never reached has no row, which is how the
table shows where a Ticket stopped.

`<version>` is the version that wrote the table (ADR-0007), in the shape
`run-summary.txt` describes.

A later Run finds this comment by its marker and carries on in it: it leaves
every section's header and table exactly as they were and writes its own
section below them, whether the Ticket was released, stranded, or resumed on the
same Host or another. A Run's transcripts go with a cloud Host's VM, so the
sections an earlier Run wrote are the only record of which Stages it ran, on
which version, and how much context they used. Each section is its own table,
so they need not agree: one an earlier version wrote with a `Turns` column is
carried forward with it, above this Run's `Context`. A Run whose own section
is already the last one — the same runId — rewrites that section rather than
starting a second. A comment an earlier version wrote, with one header and one
table, is one earlier section.

A section carries forward its header and its table and nothing else. A cloud
Host appends a `---` rule and a "Generated by Claude Code" line to every comment
written through `gh`, below the last table; whatever follows a table, in that
wording or any other, is the Host's and is left behind. So the comment holds at
most one such footer, the one the Host appended to the latest write, however
many Runs wrote to it.

The header names no Host. The runId finds it: every commit on the
`ticket-runner/lock` branch that takes the lock opens ``Held by run <runId> on
<Host>``.

One Run does not carry on: the one taking the Ticket back from a human, which is
a Ticket carrying a hand-off comment not yet marked as history. It posts a
comment of its own below the one the human read, leaving that one exactly as
they read it. So a Ticket can carry more than one of these, and the newest is
the one being written.

A Ticket handed off with no hand-off comment, a green one on a Target that
merges by hand whose every criterion was met, carries on in this comment when it
is taken back. Nothing tells the Run a human held it, and nothing failed there:
the section the human read, ending in `👤 left to a human`, stays exactly as it
was, above the new Run's.

`–` is what a cell has no answer for: a row no session reported has no
context — `setup`, `rebase`, `ci` and `merge`, a `pr` row for publishing
(`⏸ GitHub failure`, `⏸ remote unreachable`), and a `conflict` row whose Stage
result was lost (`❌ unknown`) — and the merge takes no measurable time of its
own. A Stage whose session printed no request of its own with any usage on it
has `–` too.

`<context>` is the main session's context when the Stage ended: the
`input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` of
the `usage` on the last `assistant` event of the Stage's stream whose
`parent_tool_use_id` is `null` or absent, a subagent's events naming the tool
use that started it, and whose sum is above zero, since the CLI writes its own
rate-limit and API-error messages as main-session events with all-zero usage.
The last figure is the right one with or without a compaction, after which the
peak is only where the CLI compacted. It is read from those events alone, so a
Stage the wall-clock limit stopped, or that crashed, still has one. It is
written in tokens as the Claude Code app's Context card writes its count: a
whole number below 1,000 (`850`), and from there `K` per thousand or, from
1,000,000, `M` per million, rounded to one decimal, half up, with a trailing
`.0` dropped (`107.6K`, `200K`, `1M`); a figure that rounds to `1000K` is
`1M`. It carries no percentage and no window: a token count compares across
Tickets whatever model a Target configures, and a percentage of the window
does not. ` · compacted` follows it, once however many times, when the stream
holds a `system` event with the `subtype` `compact_boundary` whose
`parent_tool_use_id` is `null` or absent: the main session compacted. The
figure is written here alone, never in the Run's log or summary, since a cloud
Host's transcripts go with its VM and this comment is what survives a cloud
Run.

`<duration>` is written as GitHub Actions writes one on a pull request's checks,
where a human already reads them: `40s` under a minute, `1m 5s` under an hour,
`3h 15m 35s` from an hour. It is rounded to the nearest second, starts at the
largest unit that is not zero, and keeps every unit below it even at zero
(`1m 0s`, `1h 0m 5s`); nothing is zero-padded. Whole minutes said little, since
most `ci` rows take one or two. The Run's length in `run-summary.txt`
stays in whole minutes: seconds change nothing over a whole Run. A section an
earlier Run wrote is carried forward as written, so one comment can read `2m` in
an older section and `1m 48s` in a newer one.

Details never go in a cell. The uncommitted paths, the unmet criteria and
their evidence belong to the hand-off comment, which is a separate comment so it
notifies the Ticket's watchers, though never the account the Run acts as, since
GitHub notifies nobody of their own comment; this one is edited in place and
notifies nobody after the first Stage.

## Outcome cells

An icon and a handful of words. `✅` passed, `❌` ended the Ticket or spent its
fix budget, `⚠️` let the Ticket go on without what its row stands for, `⏸`
released the Ticket for a later Run to resume, `👤` handed it to a human with
nothing failed.

| Stage | Outcome |
|---|---|
| setup | `❌ uncommitted work`, `⏸ remote unreachable` |
| implement | `✅ committed`, `❌ no commits`, `❌ uncommitted work`, `⏸ rate limited`, `⏸ API rate limited`, `⏸ API failure`, `⏸ out of API budget`, `❌ <why the Stage did not finish>` |
| fix | `✅ committed`, `❌ no commits`, `❌ uncommitted work`, `⏸ rate limited`, `⏸ API rate limited`, `⏸ API failure`, `⏸ out of API budget`, `❌ <why the Stage did not finish>` |
| verify | `✅ <k> met`, `✅ <k> met · <c> to CI`, `✅ <k> met · <u> unverifiable`, `✅ <k> met · <c> to CI · <u> unverifiable`, `❌ <k> unmet`, `❌ <d> defects`, `❌ <k> unmet · <d> defects`, `❌ misnumbered`, `❌ no evidence`, `❌ no verdict`, `⏸ rate limited`, `⏸ API rate limited`, `⏸ API failure`, `⏸ out of API budget`, `❌ <why the Stage did not finish>` |
| conflict | `✅ rebased`, `❌ unresolved`, `❌ uncommitted work`, `⏸ rate limited`, `⏸ API rate limited`, `⏸ API failure`, `⏸ out of API budget`, `❌ unknown` |
| rebase | `⏸ remote unreachable` |
| pr | `✅ revised`, `⚠️ left changes`, `⏸ rate limited`, `⏸ API rate limited`, `⏸ API failure`, `⏸ out of API budget`, `⚠️ <why the Stage did not finish>`, `⏸ GitHub failure`, `⏸ remote unreachable` |
| ci | `✅ passed`, `❌ failed`, `❌ conflicting`, `⚠️ no checks`, `⚠️ no workflow runs`, `❌ timed out`, ``⏸ `<command>` fails on the base branch``, `⏸ GitHub failure`, `⏸ remote unreachable` |
| merge | `✅ #<pr>`, `👤 left to a human`, `⏸ GitHub failure` |

`<d> defects` counts the defects the verify Stage found this branch made, and
reads `1 defect` for one; they fail the verdict as unmet criteria do.
`❌ misnumbered` is a verdict that left out a criterion the pipeline listed,
answered one it did not list, or answered one twice, so it graded nothing to
merge on.

`✅ <k> met` is followed by `· <c> to CI` when the verify Stage left `<c>`
criteria to CI, criteria that ask for nothing but the pull request's CI, or
some commands, to pass, which a workflow that runs on the pull request runs; and
by `· <u> unverifiable` when `<u>` criteria were unverifiable. Neither part is
written at zero. The merge ticks a criterion left to CI once CI passes.

`⚠️ no checks` is the `ci` row for a pull request GitHub listed no checks for
once the grace ran out, which merges: nothing graded the branch's code, so it is
not `✅ passed`. The criteria left to CI stay unticked and are named as
unverifiable are, and a Ticket with no met criterion is then handed off, since
no criterion has evidence to merge on.

`⚠️ no workflow runs` is the `ci` row for a pull request with no checks at the
wait's first reading when none of the workflow files on its branch can run on
it, so the wait gave it no grace. It merges too, on the same terms.

`❌ conflicting` is the `ci` row for a pull request GitHub reports as
conflicting with the base branch, which has moved since the rebase — a human
merging on GitHub meanwhile, say. GitHub runs no workflow for such a pull
request, so it is not `⚠️ no checks`, and it is not the `conflict` Stage: that
row is the rebase before the pull request, and this one comes after it.

``⏸ `<command>` fails on the base branch`` is a red CI that the branch
inherited rather than brought. The pipeline ran the Check commands once in a
clean worktree at the branch's merge-base with the base branch, and
`<command>`, the first of them the merge-base failed, failed there. Nothing
about the Ticket is wrong, so the Ticket is released with its fix budget as it
was, and this is the last row of its Run's table, like the rate limit's. It
names the command rather than the limit, because what a human does about it is
mend the base branch, which the Note on the standing Notes issue says.

`⏸ GitHub failure` and `⏸ remote unreachable` are GitHub or the git remote
failing on its own side wherever the Ticket was: a 5xx or an answer that is not
complete JSON that about a minute of tries did not mend, or git unable to
connect to or authenticate with the remote. Nothing about the Ticket is wrong,
so it is released with its fix budget as it was, and this is the last row of
its Run's table. Its Stage is the step it was on, which is why `setup` and
`rebase` have rows at all, and publishing a `pr` row: no other outcome is
written for those steps, setup's uncommitted work aside. The row says which fault it was, and the Run's last line names the
command and what it printed. A write GitHub refused here may be missing from
the table, which is why the comment is written once more when the Ticket
ends, if its last write failed.

`pr` is two things, each named by its row as `conflict` is: the pr Stage, and
publishing the pull request. The `conflict` row likewise names what it worked
on, the rebase, and its cell what happened. The pr Stage runs only on a Ticket
handed back with commits made since its hand-off, once verify passes and before
the rebase, at most once each time the Ticket is handed back; the implement and
fix Stages write every other pull request's title, body, problem and solution.
`✅ revised` is a pr Stage that finished with an answer its schema accepts, blank
answers included, which keep the recorded ones. `⚠️ left changes` is one that
left a commit or uncommitted changes: the worktree is reset to the head it
started on and its answers are dropped, since they may describe what was
discarded. `⚠️ <why the Stage did not finish>` is one that did not finish, which
leaves the recorded answers in place. Either way the Ticket goes on, without the
revision its row stands for. A pr Stage the rate limit, an API failure or the
API budget stopped releases the Ticket as any Stage does, and the Run that
resumes it still runs it. Publishing writes a `pr` row only for the faults
below, `⏸ GitHub failure` and `⏸ remote unreachable`, and its log line names
what happened, so the two read apart.

`👤 left to a human` is the `merge` row of a Ticket whose CI is green on a
Target whose config sets `merge` to `false`: the pipeline merges nothing there,
so the Ticket is handed off with its pull request as published, and this is the
last row of its Run's table.

`❌ uncommitted work` is the row of the Stage that left the worktree holding
changes no commit carries, in place of its `✅ committed` or `✅ rebased`, and a
`setup` row on a resumed Ticket, where no Stage of the Run left them. It spends
the fix budget before anything grades the branch: what lands is the branch, and
a worktree graded with work the branch lacks would pass on code the pull
request never carries.

`<why the Stage did not finish>` is the short form of a Stage failure: `timed
out`, `exited non-zero`, `invalid result`, or `failed` when the Stage came back
without saying which. A Stage's only limit is its wall-clock one. The rate
limit, a transient API failure — an API error with a 5xx status or none, after
the CLI had given up retrying it — and, on a Run started with `--api-key`, the
key out of credit or past its workspace's spend limit are the Stage failures
that are nothing about the Ticket, so they read `⏸ rate limited`, `⏸ API
failure` and `⏸ out of API budget` and are the last row of their Run's table:
the Ticket is released there, and the Run that resumes it writes its own
section below this one. The rate limit of an `--api-key` Run is the API's rather than the subscription's, and
reads `⏸ API rate limited`.

`❌ no commits` reads the same on both Stages the branch is asked about — a
session that came back having committed nothing — but it is not the same
question. implement asks whether the branch carries anything at all; fix asks
whether it grew, since implement's commits are already on it. A fix Stage that
answers no ends the Ticket where it stands, whether it spent the fix budget or
was the fix a Ticket handed back gets, spending none, for criteria a comment
added after its hand-off: a branch the Stage left as it was can only fail the
way it just did, and committing nothing is how a fix Stage hands back what only
a human can settle.

A `conflict` Stage that came back rate-limited, or stopped by an API failure or
the API budget, is still read as `✅ rebased` when it had finished the rebase
first: the worktree decides that row, so a Stage that did the job and only then
was stopped is not released.

`conflict` is the one row that can say `❌ unknown`: the worktree decides whether
the rebase was finished, so a worktree git could not be asked about leaves the
Stage's outcome unread rather than guessed at.
